stage_description: Adulthood covers roughly one to five years, the rabbit's prime. A well-cared-for house rabbit is now fully grown and settled in temperament, and typically lives eight to twelve years or more, so this long stretch is about consistency: a stable hay-based diet, daily exercise, companionship, and preventive health care. Established routines and a bonded partner keep an adult rabbit physically fit and mentally engaged.
nutrition: The foundation is unlimited grass hay such as timothy, which should make up the great majority of what an adult rabbit eats. Add a generous daily portion of varied fresh leafy greens, and only a small measured daily portion of plain pellets, far less than the hay or greens. Keep fruit and starchy treats rare, provide constant fresh water, and monitor weight so the rabbit stays trim.
activity: Adult rabbits need daily out-of-enclosure exercise, ideally several hours to run, stretch up, and explore in a safe space cleared of cables and hazards. Sustain enrichment with digging trays, tunnels, foraging toys, and fresh cardboard to chew and rearrange. Companionship matters greatly: a compatible neutered partner and things to do together prevent the boredom and obesity that come with a bare, idle enclosure.
veterinary_check_frequency: An annual wellness exam with a rabbit-savvy vet is recommended for healthy adults. Each visit should include a careful check of the teeth and mouth, weight and body condition, ears, eyes, coat, and heart, plus a review of diet and any parasite or vaccination needs in your area. Keeping a simple record of weight and appetite at home helps catch problems between visits.
dental_care: Because rabbit teeth grow throughout life, a diet dominated by unlimited grass hay is the single most important dental measure: the constant side-to-side chewing wears the crowns evenly and guards against malocclusion and painful spurs. Offer untreated wood to gnaw, and have the vet examine the back teeth yearly, since problems there are easy to miss at home.
warning_signs: A rabbit that stops eating or produces no droppings for more than about twelve hours may be in gut stasis, a true emergency, so contact a rabbit-savvy vet immediately. Other red flags include diarrhea or a dirty bottom, a bloated belly, a head tilt, laboured or open-mouth breathing, drooling, blood in the urine, sudden lethargy, or any new lump.
source_name: House Rabbit Society & Oxbow Rabbit Life Stages
